blocks.text: 12 October 2022
Prosecution Opening Speech (continued)
Wednesday, 12 October 2022
(In the presence of the jury)
Opening by MR JOHNSON (continued)
Yes, Mr Johnson.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We're moving on to counts 9 and 10, please. You'll find them in the indictment at page 4. They both concern [Baby H].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby H] was born on 22 September. So you'll remember what I told you, I think yesterday, about the way the medics count the days of life. Day 1 is the day of birth and so on. So count 10 was day 5 of [Baby H]'s life and count 11 -- I said counts 9 and 10, didn't I?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I meant counts 10 and 11, I'm sorry.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So count 10, day 5, a day of [Baby H]'s life, and count 11, day 6. So two allegations of attempted murder.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby H] had been born on 22 September at a gestational age of 34 weeks and 4 days to [Parents of Baby H]. She was delivered by C-section. She weighed 2.33 kilos, which is just over 5 pounds. Soon after birth she had breathing difficulties and she was transferred into nursery 1 at the neonatal unit. She was put on CPAP, which is one of the less invasive forms of breathing assistance.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: This is a case or [Baby H]'s is a case which is complicated to a degree by the sub-optimal treatment she received at the beginning of her life because there was what the independent experts have characterised as an unacceptable delay in intubating her, in other words putting an EG tube -- I can't even say the right term -- an ET tube -- you'll find it in the glossary; I think it's endotracheal tube -- down her throat and connecting her to a ventilator.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There was also an unacceptable delay in administering surfactant. Do you remember me telling you about that protein that is put into a baby's lungs to help -- to loosen the lungs, in effect, to make them less brittle and to help the baby's breathing?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Additionally, when [Baby H] was put on to a ventilator initially, she wasn't paralysed and she was also, at a later stage of her treatment, left with butterfly needles in her chest for prolonged periods of time, which may have punctured her lung tissues and contributed to her having -- "punctured lungs" is the phrase that you and I would use generally speaking. The phrase the medics use, and you will find it under P in the glossary, is pneumothoraces. Pneumothorax is a punctured lung, more than one, pneumothoraces.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So you can see from the indictment that we allege there are two occasions when Lucy Letby tried to kill [Baby H]. The first occasion, the one in count 10, was at about 3.25 or so in the morning of 26 September. And the second occasion was at about 00.59 in the morning of 27 September. So two consecutive night shifts is what we're talking about in general terms.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Going back to the beginning now, following [Baby H]'s birth on 22 September, [Baby H] still hadn't stabilised by the 23rd. The breathing support she was given was made more invasive from CPAP to BiPAP. We'll show you videos of all these things in due course, but just so you understand, the degree of breathing support was being increased. Then it was reduced again back to CPAP.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The important thing to recognise, really, in [Baby H]'s case, and in all the cases where this occurs, is that any form of breathing support -- or the more invasive the form of breathing support, the greater the risk of a punctured lung, a pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: On the night shift of 23 to 24 September Lucy Letby was [Baby H]'s designated nurse. [Baby H] had saturation problems through the night, in other words her blood oxygen wasn't as high as it should have been, and at 6 o'clock in the morning on the 24th [Baby H] suddenly deteriorated significantly. This isn't one of the allegations that we are making in the indictment.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby H] required ventilating by means of handbagging, and that's a process that involves the use of literally a medical practitioner or a nurse squeezing a bag to force air into the lungs and was placed back on to BiPAP, which is the slightly more invasive form of breathing support. She didn't improve and so an ET tube was put down her throat and she was put on to a ventilator at 7.45, which will be -- you will remember the change in shifts in the morning. Lucy Letby, in the normal course of events, would have been expected to go off duty at 8 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So we're still dealing with the 24th. [Baby H] deteriorated further, she required bagging further and the use of 100% oxygen
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: to support her saturations, and the pressure of the ventilator was increased and a chest X-ray taken at 8.40 on the 24th showed a left-sided pneumothorax, so a punctured lung, a punctured left lung.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The medics have concluded that it's likely that the increased pressure of the ventilator probably caused that punctured lung, so air or oxygen going in under too much pressure into the lungs causing in effect a punctured lung.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Following a further deterioration of [Baby H] later that morning, the registrar put a needle into her chest between the chest wall and the lung, so that space between the outer part of the lung and the inner part of the chest wall, and the point of that was to withdraw air that had got trapped between the inner aspect, the inner side of the chest wall, and the outer aspect, the outer side of the lung, because that compresses the lung. So that's the danger, in effect, of a punctured lung.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That needle into the chest is called a thoracocentesis. Once that air had been removed, a chest drain was put in, which had the purpose of preventing a further build-up of air between the outer side of the lung and the inner side of the chest wall.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Once that had been done, over the next few days, [Baby H] continued frequently to desaturate and significantly desaturate, but in all but two cases there was an obvious medical cause for that. The causes were variously: the punctured lung, the pneumothorax; the fact that the ET tube, the tube going down her throat, was blocked, secretions blocking the tube; suction of the ET tube; or merely handling a child can, if a child is vulnerable, cause a child, a small baby, to desaturate.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Interestingly, whilst there were two events which couldn't be explained by any of those means, the same two events also proved -- or the same two events didn't prove responsive to routine resuscitation. So these two events which are inexplicable also needed more than routine resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Those two significant and what I'll call uncharacteristic events were the two that I've told you about, the one in the early hours of the 26th and the other one in the early hours of 27 September. And both those resuscitations required a full CPR, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, with the use of adrenaline. I'm sure probably most of you know, adrenaline is a drug that's used in extreme CPR to boost blood pressure and heart rate, to bring someone back.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So dealing with the two incidents individually, ladies and gentlemen, starting with the first, the night shift of 25 into 26 September. [Baby H]'s designated nurse was Lucy Letby. Also
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: on duty that night were the registrar, Alison Ventress, the senior house officer Jessica Scott, nurses [Nurse A], Yvonne Griffiths and the nursery nurses Valerie Thomas and Elizabeth Marshall. And when [Baby H] needed the full resuscitation, Dr Gibbs, the senior consultant, had to be called in as well.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Throughout the shift, Lucy Letby undertook and recorded on the charts, some of which you've seen examples of now, the observations for [Baby H]. So her breathing rate, respiration, blood pressure, heart rate, all those sorts of things which are habitually recorded in hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby H]'s condition was such that at the beginning of the shift, those observations were being recorded every hour, but that then, because of her deteriorating condition, moved to 15minute intervals until midnight, and then back to hourly intervals from 1 o'clock in the morning.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby H]'s heart rate had risen from about 140 beats per minute, which is within the normal range for a child of her age, at 11 pm, up to 170 beats per minute at 1 o'clock and 2 o'clock. And between just after 11 pm and 2 am, she was given a blood transfusion.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 3 o'clock in the morning, her pulse had fallen back to 150 beats per minute from 170. Her respiratory rate, her breathing rate in that period, was between 45 and 55 a minute, her temperature was constant, and at 2.15 the medical notes made by Dr Gibbs, the consultant, record the fact that [Baby H]'s chest X-ray showed a re-accumulation of her left-sided pneumothorax, so that air between the inner chest wall and the outside of the left lung. So a further chest drain was inserted to relieve that pressure.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The ICU chart shows that Lucy Letby recorded having given [Baby H] a dose of morphine at 1.25 in the morning and a dose of saline at 2.50. That dose of saline was set to run for 20 minutes and therefore would have ended at 3.10. Lucy Letby, of course, therefore would have had the cover of legitimate treatment for accessing the intravenous lines for [Baby H] just before she collapsed.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 3.22, [Baby H] suffered a profound collapse and needed a full resuscitation. At the time, Dr Gibbs, the senior consultant, concluded that the cause of the collapse was unclear by contrast to what had gone before. So this time, no explanation.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At the time he concluded that the episode was caused by a shortage of oxygen, which in turn caused a profound lowering of [Baby H]'s heart rate and blood pressure.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When the registrar, Dr Ventress, arrived in response to the emergency, she found [Baby H] being bagged via the ET tube, [Baby H] had good chest movement, in other words if you're inserting using a bag, a bit like a pair of bellows for people who know what bellows are, if you're pushing air in with a bag down the tube, the ET tube, and the chest is rising, it shows that -- it's obvious, isn't it? It shows that what you're pushing in is having an effect.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that meant -- the conclusion that the doctors draw from that is that the tube was in the right position. So the tube -- the end of the tube, which is somewhere down here at the top of the lungs (indicating), was in a position that enabled air to come in and go in both sides of the lungs.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There's also a device on the end of the tube, so the end of the tube that's sort of here (indicating) in relation to the patient's mouth, called a capnograph.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And a capnograph will react, its colour will change, if carbon dioxide is coming out from the lungs. As I'm sure everybody knows, you breathe in, you absorb oxygen and you breathe out less oxygen and more carbon dioxide.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So the point of the capnograph is it shows that the air coming out has less oxygen than the air going in and more carbon dioxide, so it's an easy ready reckoner, if you like, a visual indication for the doctors, to show that things are working properly. So that was a positive sign.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby made notes in the nursing records at 4.14. She recorded a bradycardia, so a lowering of the heart rate, at 11.30, which had required Neopuffing.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She recorded the attendance of Dr Gibbs, which I have just told you about, to insert the additional chest drain. She recorded the blood transfusion that I have also told you about, at 2 o'clock, and the fact that [Baby H]'s observations were within normal range, but that [Baby H] was desaturating, so her oxygen levels were decreasing when she was handled.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Of the collapse at 3.22 she made the following record:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Profound desaturation and colour loss to 30%."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Which means [Baby H]'s saturations, which should have been in the high 90s, had gone down to 30%, which is a life-threatening level:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Good chest movement and air entry, colour change on CO2 indicator."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So the carbon dioxide indicator, the capnograph I just told you about:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Neopuff commenced in 100% oxygen and help requested. Serous fluid+++ from all three drains."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That meant there was fluid coming out of the chest drains:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Became bradycardic. Doctors crash called and resus commenced as documented."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 5.21, Lucy Letby recorded a conversation between herself, Dr Gibbs and [Baby H]'s parents. So that's the first incident.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The second incident, the one in count 11. Before that night shift of the 26th into the 27th, there had of course been a day shift, so Lucy Letby would have gone off duty at about 8 o'clock on the morning of the 26th. And during the day shift [Baby H] was relatively stable. So she'd had this life-threatening event on the night shift, and then the day shift where she was relatively stable, and the following night shift of the 26th into the 27th. And on this shift, Shelley Tomlins was the designated nurse for [Baby H].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The staff were registrar Dr Matthew Neame, senior house officer Dr Jessica Scott. The nurses were Chris Booth, who was shift leader, Shelley Tomlins, Lucy Letby, [Nurse B], and a nursery nurse, Elizabeth Marshall. So you'll see immediately the only two nurses who'd been working the previous night were Lucy Letby and the nursery nurse, Elizabeth Marshall.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So almost a complete change of staff.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby H] was still in room number 1.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In her witness statement, Nurse Tomlins said that she couldn't recall whether she'd taken a break during the shift and couldn't remember whether she'd been with [Baby H] throughout the shift. She confirmed that there would have been times when she went out of the room to get a drink or to get something from a cupboard. And the review of other children's medical records who were on the ward, on the unit that evening show that Lucy Letby had responsibility, was the designated nurse, for a child in room number 2. So [Baby H] in room 1, the other child in room 2.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There are electronic records for [Baby H], which show that Lucy Letby co-signed for some of [Baby H]'s treatments with Nurse Tomlins at just after 10 o'clock, at 10.13 and 10.38 pm, so relatively early in shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby H] suffered two sudden and unexpected episodes of profound desaturation at 00.55 and 03.30. The registrar, Dr Neame, responded to the emergency call on both occasions. On one occasion, one of those two occasions, which he thought was probably the later of the two, on arrival he saw Lucy Letby activating the Neopuff and assumed that she was actually the baby's designated nurse.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Neame took the history of what had happened from Lucy Letby, not from the designated nurse, from Lucy Letby. We suggest that this is a pretty good indicator of who it was that discovered that [Baby H] was having problems. You'll remember some of the cases I told you about, one specifically, behind the curtain where Lucy Letby discovered the problem. Well, this, we suggest, is another similar event.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Nurse Tomlins noticed that there were pink-tinged secretions around [Baby H]'s mouth. You'll remember what I told you yesterday about the swollen vocal cords of [Baby C], the bleeding round the mouth of [Baby E] when [Baby E]'s mum went to visit him at feeding time, at 9 pm, and the case of [Baby G].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Saladi, the consultant paediatrician, came in at 2.40 and no cause at the time was identified for this profound collapse either. Earlier in the shift, at just before 11 pm, the designated nurse, Shelley Tomlins, had made a note recording a profound desaturation at about 8.30, but in that case the air wasn't going through the ET tube, so that's -- there was a blockage. So that is an obvious cause. And when that was remedied, [Baby H] immediately recovered.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 9.45 in the morning there'd been a similar event which was attributed to thick secretions which were blocking the tube again. The first of the two desaturations in the shift, the one that's particularised in the indictment at 00.55, was recorded by Shelley Tomlins at 2.52 in the notes, in the nursing notes. You remember, I showed you some examples of the nursing notes yesterday. These are all documents that you will see in due course.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Shelley Tomlins noted the following. She said there had been:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "A profound desaturation to 40% despite equal bilateral entry and positive capnography."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Putting that into language that I can understand, a severe drop, profound drop, in oxygen in [Baby H]'s blood, despite the fact that there was air going down the tube into both lungs and coming out was carbon dioxide, as detected by the capnograph. So [Baby H] was desaturating, losing oxygen, despite the fact that there was unimpeded air going in and out of the ET tube.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It was also noted in the notes by Shelley Tomlins that when they suctioned the ET tube, there had been no secretions in the tube. So I suppose it's obvious, the fact that air was going in and coming out that there were no blockages, but they also checked by suctioning the tube and nothing came out. So that cannot have been the cause.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So, ladies and gentlemen, it means that, unlike the previous desaturations on this particular shift, there was no reason for what was going on.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The second of the desaturations on the shift at 3.30 also had no obvious cause, but that isn't noted in the medical records. In the context of this case it's important to differentiate between the medical records, which are the -- you or I would probably think of our medical records as including anything to do with our medical history. In the context of this case medical records are the notes made by the doctors and are divided from the nursing records which are made by, obviously, the nurses.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Neame, the registrar, made similar notes to those which had been made by Shelley Tomlins and he recorded the removal and replacement of the ET tube at about 1.05. So it's a precaution, even though it wasn't blocked, even though all the tests suggested that air was passing in and out of the lungs, they took the precaution of replacing the tube.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby H], following this second profound desaturation, was transferred to Arrowe Park Hospital on the Wirral, you'll remember the tertiary centre, the more -- the hospital that's used to dealing with more extreme cases or has the capacity to deal with more extreme cases, and she was transferred out a few hours later at 5.25 the same morning.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She actually stabilised in the ambulance that was taking her from one hospital to the other. So she improved even in the ambulance. Her mother, who was with her, speaks of her dramatic improvement as soon as she got to Arrowe Park, and the medical records bear out that improvement. She returned to the Countess of Chester 3 days later and the remainder of her time at the Countess of Chester was uneventful and she was, happily, discharged on 8 October.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Mercifully, [Baby H] has not suffered any permanent consequences from these two events in the first 2 weeks of her life. But we say, ladies and gentlemen, that it is a notable fact in [Baby H]'s case, as with others, that as soon as children were removed from the Countess of Chester and the sphere of influence of Lucy Letby, they often suddenly and remarkably recovered.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: These two incidents, and indeed the general treatment of [Baby H], have been reviewed by the independent medical experts. Dr Dewi Evans concluded that it is probable that [Baby H]'s pneumothorax, punctured lung, was a complication of her clinical condition. It was treated appropriately by the chest drain, but that there was no obvious explanation for [Baby H]'s deterioration in either the early hours of 26 or 27 September.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Sandie Bohin agreed that the punctured lungs were a combination of either prematurity, something called respiratory distress syndrome, or a combination of both, and deemed the clinical care provided as "satisfactory".
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She too expressed concern at the two events that we allege were attempts by Lucy Letby to kill [Baby H].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Because unlike earlier events, no clear cause was identified for the collapse and so profound or so extreme were the collapses that they required CPR and the use of adrenaline.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Bohin's view was those facts, the necessity for both CPR and adrenaline, showed that those collapses were more significant than the others, for which there are obvious, clear medical explanations. But Dr Bohin concluded that whilst infection almost certainly played a part in [Baby H]'s illness, it could not explain the two profound collapses because [Baby H] recovered so quickly from them. Once she was brought back, she in effect recovered.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: To be fair, Dr Bohin was critical of the way the chest drains were inserted and managed, and you'll, I dare say, be hearing a bit of evidence about that in due course.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was interviewed. In the first set of interviews in July 2018 she was asked about the incidents identified by Dr Evans on 26 and 27 September.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She confirmed that she'd been [Baby H]'s designated nurse on the 26th, she remembered [Baby H] because [Baby H] had had chest drains, which are a fairly rare thing these days, and she said she had no recollection that was independent of what was in the notes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In relation to the incident on 27 September, she said that she had not been the designated nurse and therefore assumed that she had not been caring for [Baby H]. But she did confirm her signature on the administration of some drugs to [Baby H] at 3.41 and some sucrose that was administered to [Baby H] at 3.44, and you'll remember what I've just told you of the fact that when Dr Neame arrived, there she was as the person giving the
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: history to the attending registrar, which we would suggest shows that she was the person that was there when things happened.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In June 2019 Lucy Letby identified her signatures on more medical records. In particular, she confirmed that she'd been involved in the administration of saline to [Baby H] at 2.50. That, you'll remember, ended at 3.10 and was therefore just before her collapse at 3.22.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Although having looked at the documentation, she suggested that perhaps it was [Nurse A] who had administered the saline, albeit, she, Lucy Letby, was the designated nurse on the 26th.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: On 27 September, or of 27 September, she confirmed that although she'd not been [Baby H]'s designated nurse, she had been giving her treatment at about the time [Baby H] collapsed. So yet again at the time a child collapsed inexplicably Lucy Letby was recorded as giving her treatment.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: From Lucy Letby's home address were recovered five handover sheets referring to [Baby H], two of which were for the relevant shifts that are particularised in those counts in the indictment.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's yet another case where there are some interesting Facebook searches by Lucy Letby. On 5 October 2015, so about a week after [Baby H]'s second collapse, at about 1.15 in the morning and within an overall period of 3 minutes, she searched for [Mother of Baby H], [Father of Babies E & F], and [Mother of Baby I], the mother of [Baby I], whose case is the next in the list. That day was her day off, 5 November. So on her day off, 1.15 in the morning, searching for three sets of parents, the parents of three children whose names appear in this indictment, all in a 3-minute period.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So I'm well aware that I'm starting to sound like a broken record now, ladies and gentlemen. We say this is a case that has to be looked at in the context of everything else. It fits with the pattern of unexplained collapses when Lucy Letby was there and we say it's more than an innocent coincidence that once [Baby H] was moved out of the Countess of Chester, she dramatically improved and had no further problems.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Other features that we suggest are significant are that in relation to the first incident she was the designated nurse and in relation to the second incident the collapse happened when the designated nurse was out of the room and there was Lucy Letby to explain what had happened to the registrar who attended. All things that you've heard before in previous cases. So those are the -- that's an outline of the case relating to [Baby H].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Next, [Baby I]. On the indictment, you will find [Baby I]'s name in count 12. [Baby I] was born on 7 August. She died on 23 October 2015 and this is an allegation of murder.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby I] was born in Liverpool Women's Hospital. Her gestational age was 27 weeks and her mum and dad are [Parents of Baby I]. She was born at 20.47 on 7 August. She was transferred to the Countess of Chester on the 18th. [Baby I]'s case is an extreme example, even by the standards of this overall case.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You'll remember me saying to you at the beginning that Lucy Letby made repeated attempts to kill some of these children. This is a case where we allege Lucy Letby tried four times and succeeded on the fourth attempt.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby I] was resilient, but ultimately at the fourth attempt Lucy Letby succeeded in killing her. [Baby I] weighed 970 grams at birth, 2 pounds and 2 ounces.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Although she was small, she was born in good condition, and despite the fact that she was so premature she did very well from the very beginning.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was intubated and ventilated for the first 10 hours of her life, but then taken off the ventilator and supported with CPAP, which is one of the less invasive ways of supporting breathing. She didn't have any significant lung disease and she was being fed initially through the nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the first few weeks of her life she did have a few problems, but, as you will see in other cases, these all had obvious causes and were all resolved. So it was almost 2 months later, 29 September, when she was 8 weeks old, that the ongoing clinical concerns that had existed had diminished. [Baby I] had no breathing problems, she was in air -- in other words she wasn't having any supplemental oxygen to improve her saturations -- she was gaining weight, and she was being fed using bottles and through the NGT.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: 29 September was a couple of days, 2 days after Lucy Letby's second attempt to kill [Baby H].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And lest you have forgotten, it was a week or so after events 2 and 3 for [Baby G].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So the first attempt by Lucy Letby to kill [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: On 30 September Lucy Letby worked a long day and that's a day shift that lasts 8 until 8 and she was [Baby I]'s designated nurse. [Baby I] was doing so well that she was in room number 3,
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: with two other children, and Lucy Letby was the designated nurse for all three of the children in room 3.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Despite the fact that she had three babies to care for, Lucy Letby was also involved that shift with both [Baby H] and [Baby G]. Other staff on duty were the consultant Dr Gibbs, John Gibbs, the registrar [Dr A], two -- I think three -- SHOs on that day shift, Doctors Peter Fielding, Charlotte Newton and Dr Lucy Hunt. The nurses were [Nurse B], who was the shift leader, Lucy Letby, Laura Eagles, Melanie Taylor, Ashleigh Hudson, Kate Bissell and Bernadette Butterworth, and the nursery nurses Jean Peers and Lisa Walker. You can see already there were generally more staff on during the day than would be on at night.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: According to [Baby I]'s mum, [Mother of Baby I], Lucy Letby expressed some concern about [Baby I] to her and indicated that [Baby I] would need to be reviewed by a doctor. When she made the notes in the nursing notes though, Lucy Letby reversed this concern and said that it had been [Mother of Baby I] who had expressed concern about [Baby I] to her. And what Lucy Letby wrote in the notes was -- this is of [Mother of Baby I]'s abdomen:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Mum feels it's more distended [swollen] to yesterday and that [Baby I] is quiet. Not on monitor but nil increased work of breathing."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So it's a point you might want to bear in mind when we get to [Baby I]'s case. Who was raising the concern here? Was it Lucy Letby to cover what she planned to do?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Mother of Baby I] says it was Lucy Letby. Or was it as Lucy Letby recorded in the notes? You know what we say about Lucy Letby's notes from some of the other cases.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can I just show you the feeding chart, please, which is J14457. It's not the feeding chart, it's the nursing notes, I beg your pardon.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You'll be very used to these by the time we finish, ladies and gentlemen, I'm sure you already know from what you've seen previously that these are the nursing notes. It says at the top "Patient notes: nurse notes".
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You can see this is a note made on 30 September at 13.36 and perhaps ending at 13.48. LL of course Lucy Letby:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Written for care given from 8 to present."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So this is covering a period from the start of the shift:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Emergency equipment checked, fluids calculated. [Baby I] nursed on a hot cot, initially set at 36.5 degrees."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then sets out her temperature. Then a bit further down:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Abdomen appears full and slightly distended, soft to touch."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's a good sign, soft on touch:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "[Baby I] straining++. Bowels have been opened. Mum feels it is more distended to yesterday and that [Baby I] is quiet. Appears generally pale. Not on monitor but nil increased work of breathing. Handling well and waking for feeds. Doctors asked to review to continue with current plan."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Handling well and waking for feeds", a good sign, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: A review took place at 3 pm, so an hour and 20 minutes or so after these notes were made. By then, [Baby I] appeared mottled in colour with a distended abdomen and prominent veins, but she was still breathing unassisted in air.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We can move on to the feeding chart now, please, at 14780. I'm going to tell you what they say first of all and then I'll point out the bit -- here we are, perfect.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So feeding chart. If you look at the far right-hand column, ladies and gentlemen, you can see Lucy Letby's signature and underneath that her initials. If we go back towards the lefthand side of the chart, in the second column we've got the times, 00.30, 3.30, 7 o'clock, 10 o'clock, 1 o'clock, 4 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We can see in the next column what [Baby I] was being fed:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "EBM [which means expressed breast milk]/fort [or fortifier]..."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And that's a thickener that is put into the breast milk. I'll let the doctors explain why that's done.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the next column, the amount, 35 millilitres, 35.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then the route. What we see is B for bottle, NGT for nasogastric tube. Then in the next column:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Vomit ASP."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: This relates to -- do you remember me telling you yesterday that before feeding a child, a baby, particularly a premature baby, the nurse would draw up through the tube using a syringe -- the other end of the tube sitting in the stomach, would draw up from the stomach to see what comes up. And if there is a large
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: quantity of undigested milk before you're about to feed a child then that's a bad sign, so the child would not be fed.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: What you see here at -- well, there are no entries at all in the first few, in the first four lines. In the line at 1 pm we see 5 millilitres were aspirated and a pH of 5, so that's a measure of -- anyone who knows anything about chemistry, pH gives you the acidity or alkalinity of something, and you can see in the 4 o'clock feed 3 millilitres were drawn up before the feed. But that wasn't a concern and so [Baby I] was fed, hence the figures in the column two to the left, 35 and 35.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: What Lucy Letby recorded there at 4 o'clock, therefore, is that she fed [Baby I] 35 millilitres of expressed breast milk at 4 o'clock and that she fed it to [Baby I] down the NG tube because, if you look in the comments column that's just to the left of her initials, [Baby I] was asleep.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: An emergency crash call was put out for [Baby I] at 4.30 because [Baby I] had vomited, desaturated, her heart rate dropped, and she was struggling to breathe. You can see a note in Lucy Letby's handwriting, 4.30:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Large vomit+ [so emphasis] and apnoea [in other words not breathing] NBM."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "NBM" means nil by mouth.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby I]'s airway had to be cleared, she was given breathing support, and she was moved into room number 1.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: An X-ray, taken at about 5.30/5.40, revealed a massive amount of gas in her stomach and in her bowel, and her lungs appeared squashed. You remember me telling you yesterday about the diaphragm? If you overfill the stomach, like a balloon it expands, pushes up on the diaphragm and the diaphragm in turn squashes the lungs, so reduces the capacity for a small child to breathe.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So the effect of this gas that we say had been injected into [Baby I] through the nasogastric tube, into her stomach, was to in effect splint her diaphragm and impede her capacity to breathe.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Harkness, the registrar, recorded having seen [Baby I] at 4.30, and [Baby I] had suffered a respiratory arrest, she'd stopped breathing. She was pale, she was distressed, her abdomen was described as "distended and hard". Her heart rate was low, she was struggling to breathe, and what he wrote in the notes was that the NGT was aspirated, in other words out again -remember this is only half an hour after she'd been fed -- and
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: produced air+++ -- so in half an hour, air+++ had got in there — and 2 millilitres of milk. So if 35 went in, there was a vomit, leaving 2. This is an interesting comparison to one of the cases I told you about yesterday, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: As soon as that air was removed from [Baby I], the crisis passed. You'll remember, won't you, [Baby C], [Baby E], [Baby G]? [Baby G] was the projectile vomit on to the chair, do you remember?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby's shift ended at 8 pm and the handover to the nurse for the night shift took place between 7.30 and 8.00, and at 7.30, at the beginning of the handover, the notes record that Lucy Letby adjusted [Baby I]'s glucose infusion and gave her an injection of saline; and within moments you know what happens, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby I] deteriorated again.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: But as I've already said, [Baby I] was resilient and overnight, once removed from the orbit of Lucy Letby, [Baby I]'s condition improved. In the period after that shift, she enjoyed a period of stability and so stable was [Baby I] that by 11 October, she wasn't even on a monitor for her heart rate or her respiration rate.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was doing so well that she didn't need to be monitored.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Incident 2 was on the night shift beginning 12 October. Nurse Ashleigh Hudson was [Baby I]'s designated nurse on this shift, [Baby I] was in nursery 2, she was with two other babies, and Lucy Letby had a baby in nursery 1. There were two other babies in nursery 1 being looked after by Laura Eagles. So putting that a different -- this is important in this case. Three babies in nursery 1, two being looked after by Laura Eagles, one by Lucy Letby. Three babies in nursery 2, all being looked after by Ashleigh Hudson.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The staff on duty that shift were registrar Dr Matthew Neame, the senior house officer was Dr Ekaterina Clegg. The nurses, the shift leader was Caroline Oakley. Together with Lucy Letby, the other two nurses were Ashleigh Hudson and Laura Eagles, who I have already mentioned, and the nursery nurse was Janet Cox.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby I] was well at the beginning of the shift. She was being fed by bottle every 4 hours and at 1.30 in the morning she took a 55-millilitre bottle of breast milk.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At about 3 o'clock on 13 October, Ashleigh Hudson left the nursery temporarily. So she's got the three in nursery 2, including [Baby I]. She leaves. What she remembers is that she
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: asked either Lucy Letby or Caroline Oakley to listen out for [Baby I]. Does that remind you of things I've already told you about?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Nurse Hudson, the records show, went into room number 1, into nursery 1, where Lucy Letby had her child. What Nurse Hudson did, the records show, is she helped Laura Eagles with one of the children in room number 1. So when you're wondering who it would have been that Nurse Hudson asked to help out by supervising [Baby I] and the other two in room 2, it's a fairly obvious inference to draw, isn't it, given that Lucy Letby was already in room 1? "Do you mind just going into room 2 to keep an eye on the babies while I help here in your room?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Whether or not that's right, whether or not the inference that I'm inviting you to consider is right, Ashleigh Hudson remembers that when she returned to room 2 at about 3.20, Lucy Letby was standing in the doorway of the room. The room was darkened, because it was night, and as soon as Ashleigh Hudson appeared, Lucy Letby said to her that [Baby I] looked pale.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Nurse Hudson then turned on the light and saw that [Baby I] appeared to be at the point of death and wasn't breathing.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When she reconsidered it later, months, years later, she thought possibly [Baby I] was breathing at least once every 20 seconds, and it may be that that's what she thinks because, if she hadn't been breathing once every 20 seconds, the apnoea alarm would have gone off and there was no alarm sounding. Of course, the alternative might be somebody had silenced or turned off the alarm.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You may want to consider that as a possibility.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You might also want to wonder how it is that Lucy Letby, from the doorway of a darkened room, could see into a cot and that [Baby I] looked pale. This is yet another feature of the case that will repeat.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sorry, Mr Johnson.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
DARTS has just gone off. It's the digital recording system.
Sometimes the clock stops but the system...
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's rebooting or trying to reboot.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
Maybe we could take an early break.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: (Pause)
In terms of a break, we will have a break: you choose an appropriate moment from now on.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, ladies and gentlemen, what Ashleigh Hudson remembers is certainly right. It's right because Lucy Letby made a note at 8 o'clock at the end of the shift -- 8.10, actually, at the end of the shift. I'll just show you that now, please. It's 14504.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She wasn't [Baby I]'s designated nurse, you will remember, but here she is making a note. To be fair, I think care was transferred to Lucy Letby at a later stage. Anyway. Here's the note made at between 07.59 and 8.10:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "[Baby I] noted to be pale in cot by myself at 03.20. Nurse Hudson present. Apnoea alarm in situ and had not sounded. On examination [Baby I] centrally white, minimal shallow breaths followed by gasping observed. Ventilation breaths."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Neame, the registrar, was beeped at 3.23. When he got to [Baby I] he saw that the nurses were giving her full CPR. He repositioned [Baby I]'s ET tube, [redacted].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The consultant, Dr Newby, arrived a few minutes later and gave [Baby I] adrenaline, intubated her and ventilated her.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And an X-ray showed gross gas swelling throughout her bowel and signs of something called chronic lung disease of prematurity.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So in other words, [Baby I] had, on this occasion, the same problem that she'd had back on 30 September when Lucy Letby had fed her and there was Lucy Letby again when it recurred out of the ether. And yet in the intervening 2 weeks, [Baby I] had been absolutely fine.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The medical team at the time felt that the swelling of [Baby I]'s abdomen, her stomach, had affected her ability to expand her chest and that was the cause of the deterioration. What they appeared not to have considered so much is how the stomach got distended or swollen in the first place. And both the nursing and the medical staff commented on a bruise-like discolouration to the right of the sternum, the breastbone, and assumed that was a result of the chest compressions that had been given to [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The category of nursing care was raised a level and ironically, Lucy Letby then became [Baby I]'s designated nurse because she was the more qualified.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Neame's medical notes record that not only had the ET tube been displaced at the time [Baby I] had collapsed but also, at 4.25 in the morning, the nasogastric tube had curled in her oesophagus, so that was misplaced as well, and that happening to the NG tube would mean that that would stop any pressure in the stomach from the gas coming out through the tube: that gas that we say Lucy Letby had put in there couldn't come out because the tube was curled.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that's incident 2. [Baby I] survived.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Incident 3. The night shift of 13 to 14 October.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was [Baby I]'s designated nurse and [Baby I] was her only responsibility that night, she had no other children to care for. The other staff on duty were the registrar Dr Neame, Dr Clegg was the house officer, Nurse Caroline Oakley the shift leader, Lucy Letby working with Joanne Williams and Laura Eagles, and the nursery nurse Janet Cox. You'll get all these in lists, ladies and gentlemen. You don't need to write them down if you feel you don't want to.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby I] was in room number 1 with at least a couple of other babies. On 14 October both Lucy Letby and Dr Neame recorded that [Baby I] had increasing abdominal distension. She had discolouration to the right and she was sensitive to touch between 5 am and 5.55. In other words, coming up towards the end of the shift. An X-ray taken at 6.05 shows that she had widespread gas, which was swelling her stomach, and it was sufficient to splint the diaphragm. So the same problem happening again. This prevented [Baby I] breathing properly, it led to her desaturating again, and yet again she had to be resuscitated.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So same nurse, same problem. A problem that didn't occur when Lucy Letby wasn't about.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 7 am, [Baby I] had a significant desaturation with a lowered heart rate, which required full resuscitation, so CPR, adrenaline. At 7.10 Dr Neame recorded this in the notes:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "... then desaturating again despite good [air entry]..."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do you remember me telling you about air entry before? So sats crashing but air coming in and out.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "... despite good [air entry], chest wall movement and negative cold light."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We'll hear about a thing called a cold light test.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's a test they do to see if there's a punctured lung, a pneumothorax, so negative means there's no evidence of a punctured lung.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 7.45, so right at the end of the shift:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Heart rate below 60. CPR initiated. Capnography positive."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So carbon dioxide was coming out of [Baby I], so there was the gas exchange within the lungs, but despite that, still in a life-threatening situation:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Chest wall movement and equal..."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And [Baby I] was bought back from the brink of death right at the end of the shift at 7.58.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby's notes were made at about 8.45. She recorded this:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "At 5 o'clock abdomen noted to be more [distended] and firmer in appearance with areas of discolouration spread on right-hand side. Veins more prominent, gradually requiring 100% oxygen. Blood gases poor as charted. Nil obtained from NG tube throughout. Continued to decline. Re-intubated at approximately 7 am. Initially responded well. Resuscitation commenced as documented in medical notes. Night and day staff members present."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that was the third attempt that Lucy Letby made to kill [Baby I]. [Baby I] experienced a transient, a temporary desaturation, at just after 9 o'clock that night, and respiratory difficulties on the morning of 15 October. And she was transferred to Arrowe Park Hospital, the tertiary centre.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She had an episode where her heart rate dropped and she desaturated, but after that she quickly stabilised.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So as before, here we have another child suffering lifethreatening problems and a speedy recovery once removed from Chester, and in due course was then returned back to Chester and on 17 October, and [Baby I] had, when she came back to Chester on the 17th, had 5 good days of progress, a period that coincided with the absence from work of Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The night shift of 22 to 23 October.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Ashleigh Hudson was the designated nurse for [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby I] was in room 1 with at least one other child.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby had a child in room number 3. Other staff on duty that night were on-call consultant Dr Gibbs, registrar was Dr Chang, the SHO was Dr Laddie, the nurses were Ashleigh Hudson, Melanie Taylor and Christopher Booth, obviously with Lucy Letby, and also the nursery nurse Val Thomas.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Between 8 o'clock that evening and [Baby I]'s collapse, the only entry Lucy Letby made in any child's records in that unit that night were those of her designated infant in room number 3. And she recorded having fed that child, who I'll call MCA, and taking the child's observations at 9 pm. It therefore appears from the records she made at least that it was a slow night for Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So far as [Baby I] was concerned, at 11 pm [Baby I]'s fluid balance chart was noted by her designated nurse, Ashleigh Hudson. At just before midnight [Baby I] became unsettled and Nurse Hudson and Lucy Letby attended to her, but [Baby I] collapsed and required cardiac compressions.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Chang, the on-call registrar, attended, followed by Dr Gibbs, the consultant. Dr Gibbs arrived at about 00.15 on 23 October, and noted that CPR was underway, [Baby I] had a mottled blue appearance of the trunk and her peripheries and, as on previous occasions, the contemporaneous medical notes record that when [Baby I] was intubated there was good colour change of the capnograph, the carbon dioxide detector. After 5 minutes of CPR [Baby I]'s saturations picked up to 100%, she was then ventilated when Dr Gibbs arrived, and once again the X-ray showed a massive dilation of her bowel, which was noted as a "large stomach bubble", and [Baby I] was successfully resuscitated at that stage and recovered to the extent that she was rooting -- rooting in this context means that she wants to be fed, sucking, pouting as if she wants some milk -- and she was fighting the ventilator, in other words had sufficient about her to be breathing not in sync with the ventilator but breathing for herself and against the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So because of that, at 00.45, the ET tube was removed. At 1.06, Nurse Hudson left the nursery, and you know what I'm going to say next, don't you? She responded to [Baby I]'s alarm and Lucy Letby was standing by the incubator. [Baby I] was very distressed and Nurse Hudson wanted to intervene, but Lucy Letby said that they'd be able to sort it out. "Don't worry, we'll sort it out, we'll settle her." I'm not saying that's a direct
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: quotation of what she said, but what she said was, "We will settle the baby".
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby I] then collapsed. This, if you sort of park this exchange, mirrors what will happen in one of the later cases, a lad called [Baby O], about 6 months later.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Chang arrived at 1.12, he led the attempts to resuscitate [Baby I] -- sorry, she led the attempts to resuscitate [Baby I]. She was joined by Dr Gibbs at 1.25, who noted purple and white mottling. As before, the capnograph, the CO2, detector, on the ET tube, suggested that air was getting in and out of [Baby I]'s lungs, but all resuscitative efforts were unsuccessful, and at 2.10 treatment was withdrawn.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby I] was pronounced dead at 2.30 and in the immediate aftermath of her death, her parents were taken into a private room. Ashleigh Hudson and Lucy Letby asked if [Mother of Baby I] wanted to bathe her daughter.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: As [Mother of Baby I] bathed her recently departed child, Lucy Letby came into the room, and in the words of [Mother of Baby I], "was smiling and kept going on about how she was present at [Baby I]'s first bath and how much [Baby I] had loved it".
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: This case was referred to the coroner.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: A post-mortem examination was carried out by Dr Kokai on 26 October. The cause of death was recorded as:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Hypoxic ischaemic damage of brain and chronic lung due to prematurity and extreme prematurity."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: One of the findings at the post-mortem examination was that all the loops of [Baby I]'s bowel showed what the medics call "significantly dilated lumen due to increased air content". In layman's terms that means expanded, like a partially inflated balloon.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There were no signs of NEC, that bowel disorder, or any other bowel problem, and an examination of [Baby I]'s brain showed signs of earlier hypoxic ischaemic damage, in other words brain damage from oxygen starvation, and in other words the earlier attempts to kill [Baby I] had caused brain damage resulting from a shortage of oxygen.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And testing for a battery of viruses proved negative.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The independent experts. Dr Evans, he acknowledges this is a highly complicated case, but was of the view that [Baby I]'s deteriorations on 30 September, on 13 October, when he thought
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: the apnoea monitor must have been switched off or tampered with, on 22 and 23 October are all consistent with the deliberate administration of a large amount of air into [Baby I]'s stomach through the NG tube.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Evans also believes that [Baby I] was given an amount of air injected into her bloodstream on or just before and after midnight on 22 to 23 October, and in support of that opinion he refers to [Baby I] screaming, quickly followed by her collapse.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Bohin agreed with Dr Evans and made the point that the findings at post-mortem excluded NEC, this bowel disease, as being the problem.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Marnerides, the independent pathologist, concluded that the constellation of findings would strongly indicate that [Baby I] died due to unnatural causes, having been submitted to repeated, separate episodes of excessive injection of air into her stomach and intestines.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby, having been arrested, was interviewed.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In July 2018 she confirmed that she had been [Baby I]'s designated nurse on 30 September. She confirmed that she'd given [Baby I] a feed via her NG tube at 4 o'clock and said she couldn't remember the circumstances in which the crash call had been put out at 4.30. You remember that's the chart I showed you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby confirmed that on the night shift of 12 to 13 October she had taken over the care of [Baby I] at 3.20, after [Baby I] had had an "episode". With regards to the events of 14 October, she said she had no independent recollection. She said she had no recollection of the events surrounding [Baby I]'s death and she said her view was that Arrowe Park had brought or sent back [Baby I] too quickly to the Countess of Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In June 2019 she was asked about a sympathy card that she had sent to [Baby I]'s parents. She said that to send a card -- for a nurse to send a card was not normal. Indeed, this was the only time she said she had ever done it. But it was not often that the nurses got to know a family as well as they had known [Baby I]'s family. She accepted that she had kept an image of that card on her phone.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She denied giving [Baby I] air through her NGT. She was asked about the occasion on 13 October when [Baby I] had desaturated in the dark and she said that the first time she had realised was when the lights were illuminated but couldn't remember why she and Ashleigh had gone into the room and you'll remember what was in the note I showed you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She challenged Ashleigh Hudson's account, so she didn't agree with what Ashleigh Hudson said, and continued by saying:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Maybe I spotted something that Ashleigh wasn't able to spot."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Because, as she said, she was "more experienced than Ashleigh".
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She denied that Ashleigh Hudson had left her with the responsibility for caring for [Baby I] on that night.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You'll remember what I've said about that.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the interview of November 2020 she was asked about the text messages she'd sent to [Nurse A] on 14 October in which she had asked to be assigned to [Baby I]'s care on the following shift. She said that she didn't recall the detail of those messages. And as with other cases, she was asked why she had taken an interest in [Baby I]'s parents on Facebook. Her response was that she didn't recall doing it.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, you will remember what I said to you earlier this morning, ladies and gentlemen, about that 3-minute period in the early hours of one of her days off when she searched for [Baby I]'s parents, [Baby H]'s parents and [Babies E & F]'s parents.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So ladies and gentlemen, in summary, [Baby I] was born very early and very small, but she survived for 2 months, for the first 2 months of her life, and was doing well by the time Lucy Letby got her hands on her.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: What happened to [Baby I] following the pattern -- or followed the pattern of what had happened to others before and what was yet to happen to others that I'll be telling you about later.

blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

Incident 2, the designated nurse fed [Baby I], left her and returned to find Lucy Letby coolly watching [Baby I], who was in crisis. Incident 3, similar to incident 1 but without the vomit, [Baby I] pumped up with air. And finally, the fatal incident, incident 4, [Baby I] pumped up with air when the designated nurse was away from her and the designated nurse returning in response to the alarm and finding Lucy Letby standing over her.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Eight days after the death of [Baby I], was born [Baby J] on 31 October 2015. [Baby J] was 32 weeks plus 2 days gestation. Once she started to breathe regularly, she was initially stable. However, it was discovered that she had a necrotic and perforated bowel.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was a child, and the only child in this case, who really did have NEC, that bowel disorder.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The following day, she was transferred to Alder Hey Children's Hospital in Liverpool and there she had what's called a bowel resection and ileostomy with an external stoma and bag. What that means is, ladies and gentlemen, that they opened her up, found the bit of dead bowel, cut the dead bit out and then created a stoma, which is an exit for the bowel in the wall of the abdomen, which is where you would have the bag to collect the faeces. But they don't do that in the sense -- what they tend to do is they also have an entry point from the healthy end of the bowel and they do what they call recycling the stools. So stools will be produced by the digestive process, will come out of the exit point and will then be put into the entry point to come out the normal way. Once that has been established then they tend to have a further operation in which the child is reopened and the two healthy ends of bowel are stitched together, which means that the child will live a normal life -- normal in the sense of not having to have a bag. So that's the mechanical explanation which no doubt will be given in much better and more accurate terms by the expert witnesses in due course.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Having had that operation, [Baby J] recovered well and she was returned to the Countess of Chester on 10 November and her
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: clinical condition was stable. She had to help with her nutrition a line called a Broviac line, which I won't try to explain, but it's an unusual type of line that is inserted under surgery. So that was done at the same time that [Baby J] had the bowel operation.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The issue of the stoma and that in combination with a Broviac line was something that was unusual and many of the staff in the Countess of Chester were not familiar with that sort of thing.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: On 16 November, so the birth plus 17 days, the medical notes reflect that [Baby J] was well, she was breathing in air, her saturations, her oxygen saturations, were 100%, her temperature was normal, her heart rate and breathing rate were healthy. But she suffered an unexplained collapse in the early hours of 27 November.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That night shift, the nurses on duty were Mary Griffith, Lucy Letby, Caroline Oakley, Nicola Dennison, Laura Eagles and Vicky Blamire, and this was now 5 weeks after the death of [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Before she went to work for that shift, Lucy Letby exchanged text messages with one of her colleagues, and it seems that she wasn't happy with her working conditions and she referred to the difficulties of looking after babies who'd only needed feeding support.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So in other words, the babies in room 3 and room 4. She wasn't happy about that. [Baby J] was one of those and it appears, we suggest, that working in nurseries 3 and 4 was not sufficiently stimulating for Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: On this particular night shift, Nurse Dennison was the designated nurse for [Baby J], who by this stage was in room 4, ready to go home. Lucy Letby's charge was in a different room and although she wasn't designated to [Baby J], the notes suggest that Lucy Letby got herself involved with [Baby J]. She co-signed for the administration of medication, just after midnight, and to be fair it may well be that because Nurse Dennison was a band 4 nurse and therefore not sufficiently qualified to give intravenous medication to [Baby J], that may be the reason why Lucy Letby got involved. But whether or not that is the reason, [Baby J] was well and she was on 4-hourly observations. We've seen some cases, haven't we, with 15 minutes? So to give you a contrast, here was [Baby J] on 4hourly observations.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby J] was well, but after a feed at about 4.40 that morning, Nurse Dennison thought that [Baby J] became pale and mottled. And shortly after, she left the room for a short time and, when
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: she returned, Nurse Griffiths (sic) was helping [Baby J] with [Baby J]'s breathing.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Nurse Griffiths can't remember the incident or how her involvement came about, and an examination of the records of all the other children on the unit at the time showed the last thing Lucy Letby recorded herself doing before the collapse of [Baby J] was at about 3 o'clock, and there's data from the door fob system, the security pass system that the staff use, which suggests that following that event at 3 o'clock, Lucy Letby had come back into the neonatal unit at 3.47.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So it may well be that she'd had a break between 3 o'clock and 3.47.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So I've told you about her desaturation. It was just after 5 o'clock, 5 am, that [Baby J] suffered a further desaturation and the decision was made to move her to the high dependency part of the unit in room number 2.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At that point Mary Griffith took over [Baby J]'s care and began to monitor her condition. Dr Verghese, one of the registrars, was called and she examined [Baby J] -- he examined [Baby J]. Dr Verghese was told that [Baby J] had suffered two profound desaturations which had required breathing support from the nursing staff and he examined [Baby J] and found that she was working hard to breathe, although otherwise she had recovered well and she was screened for infection and her feeds were stopped.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 6.56, so coming up to the end of the shift, [Baby J]'s alarm activated and she suffered another episode. Nurse Griffith responded and was joined quickly by Lucy Letby. [Baby J]'s saturation and heart rate had both dropped and she required help. Dr Gibbs was present on the unit by this time and he took control and describes [Baby J]'s oxygen levels as "dropping to unrecordable levels" and her circulation as "poor". And he noticed also symptoms of a seizure in that [Baby J]'s arms were stiff, her fists were clenched and her eyes were deviating to the left.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 7.20 Lucy Letby signed a chart for the administration of a 10% glucose infusion and the co-signer for that was Mary Griffith. If we just look at this, please, it's page 16244.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We can see there highlighted in yellow are the signatures, Lucy Letby's signature above and Mary Griffith's rather smaller signature in the same box below and those two signatures replicated in the following line, which contains another prescription that has been stricken through.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Four minutes later, 7.24, [Baby J] again collapsed.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So within minutes of an infusion started by Lucy Letby, [Baby J] collapsed and it was handover time and so there were numerous members of staff on the unit. Two shifts' worth of staff on the unit at this stage. Dr Gibbs had again helped to resuscitate [Baby J]. Again on this occasion [Baby J]'s fists were clenched, her eyes were rolling to the left and mercifully [Baby J] recovered satisfactorily from that collapse. But Dr Gibbs could offer no explanation for what had happened from the results of various tests that were undertaken and he considered the incidents unexplained.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: These episodes or this episode was reviewed by the independent experts. Dr Evans described the collapse at 7.11 as unexpected, without any straightforward explanation, and said that it was:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Of concern and consistent with some form of obstruction of her airways, such as smothering."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby J] was well beforehand, there was no evidence of infection and she recovered soon after.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The symptoms of a seizure or a fit, this clenching of the fists, stiffening of arms and eyes deviating to the left, suggests that the brain was deprived of oxygen and raised the prospect therefore that [Baby J]'s airway had been obstructed. Ever since [Baby J] has never suffered a seizure. In a later statement Dr Evans said:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Whilst I have concerns regarding the suddenness of [Baby J]'s deterioration on 27 November, one cannot rule out the presence of infection, despite the normal inflammatory markers at the time of the collapse episode."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And noted also the presence of the stoma, this exit and entry of the bowel, which could have been a source for organisms that caused a systemic infection.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Evans reviewed the case later, [Baby J]'s case later, and persisted in the view that airway obstruction was the most likely cause of [Baby J]'s collapse and concluded that that couldn't be because a tube was blocked because [Baby J] hadn't been intubated at this stage, she was getting no ventilatory support at all.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He excluded the possibility of [Baby J] having inhaled milk, because [Baby J] had been on normal feeds for some time, had coped well and if that had been the source of the problem then her airways would have required clearing, which they didn't.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Also he made the point that if [Baby J] had inhaled milk she wouldn't have recovered so quickly.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Bohin also considered the issue of infection in relation to this occasion. She concluded that the issue could not have been infection because there had been no, what she categorised as, soft signs. By that, she's referring to a sort of gradual deterioration which you would expect if this collapse had been the result of infection.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: By contrast, she made the point this was a sudden collapse and it was so sudden that whatever happened caused her brain to be starved of oxygen, which in turn had caused the seizures. She then recovered quickly and the inflammatory markers, in other words the things that they look for in your blood to see if you have an infection, were low.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was interviewed about this. She said she had little recollection of [Baby J] but did remember the Broviac line, and she said that the level of interest in [Baby J]'s treatment was unusual. She confirmed contact with [Baby J] on the occasions that had been recorded in the medical records but denied doing anything to cause her any harm.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In 2020, when she was interviewed, Lucy Letby was asked why it was she'd searched Facebook for [Baby J]'s parents on 17 December 2015. She said, "I don't remember doing that".
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, ladies and gentlemen, our case is straightforward here. We suggest that it is highly significant that children within the orbit of Lucy Letby persistently and consistently suffered unexplained collapses. Sometimes the evidence of her hand at work is more obvious than others and it's remarkable that on many occasions when children who'd suffered unexpected spectacular and life-threatening collapses were removed from her orbit, they had exceptional recoveries. [Baby J]’s case is one where, we suggest, that its parallels with other cases tell you what happened and who was responsible.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON
