blocks.text: Welcome back, ladies and gentlemen. Can we go to the indictment again, please, at page 6, counts 15 and 16. You'll see named [Babies L & M], two twins, [Babies L & M]. I'll deal with [Baby L]'s case first.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Both [Babies L & M] were born on 8 April 2016.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the days before they were born, Lucy Letby moved into her new house at 41 Westbourne Road in Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby L] was born at 10.13 in the morning of 8 April.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He and his brother were 33 weeks and 2 days gestation.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby L] was the first born and it's the prosecution case that Lucy Letby attacked [Baby L] first with insulin -- and you'll remember [Baby F] is the other insulin baby -- and then, whilst the attack on [Baby L] was underway, she also attacked [Baby M].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: As with all neonates, so children just born, [Baby L]'s blood glucose levels were tested at regular intervals.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Between 34 minutes of age and 6 hours and 20 minutes of age, [Baby L]'s blood glucose level was noted to be low, so hypoglycaemia. That deficiency, that low reading, was marginal and considered to be naturally occurring given his prematurity and small size.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He was treated for it with a sugar infusion, a dextrose infusion. It's in a clear plastic bag and hangs from a thing by the side of the bed and runs through a tube into the body. That was signed for by Nurse Lucy Letby and Nurse Davies at 11 o'clock. His condition improved and by the night shift that ended at breakfast time on Saturday, 9 April, [Baby L] was stable.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: On the Saturday day shift, so this is the day after Lucy Letby had hooked up the sugar or the glucose infusion, the Saturday
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: day shift Lucy Letby came on duty at 7.30 in the morning. The other staff on duty or the other nursing staff on duty, I should say, were [Nurse B], who was the shift leader, Mary Griffith, Belinda Simcock and Ashleigh Hudson with the nursery nurse Angela McShane.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So it follows that on duty on this day shift on 9 April were only two people who were on duty when [Baby F] was poisoned with insulin. Lucy Letby was one and the other was Belinda Simcock.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Mary Griffith was the designated nurse for [Baby L] and [Baby M], who were both in room number 1, and the designated nurse for the other two babies in room number 1 that Saturday morning was Lucy Letby. By this time Lucy Letby was supposed only to be working day shifts because the consultants were concerned about the correlation between her presence and unexplained deaths and life-threatening episodes on the night shifts.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the hours that followed Lucy Letby's arrival that morning, [Baby L]'s glucose levels fell to abnormally low levels and throughout the day he was given additional doses of glucose in an attempt to correct that low blood sugar, but they proved ineffective.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The reason for [Baby L]'s hypoglycaemia, low blood sugar, was found in a test performed on his blood sample, which was taken mid-afternoon at 3.45 that Saturday, 9 April. The sample had to be sent to a laboratory at the Royal Liverpool teaching hospital and, because of that, there was a delay in the doctors at the Countess of Chester receiving the results until some time after [Baby L]'s condition had improved. So [Baby L] -- by the time they got the results back, the problem had been sorted.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It seems that although the results of the test were grossly abnormal, nothing was done about it because by the stage the report came back, [Baby L] was well.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: As with the case of [Baby F] before him, the results revealed a very high level of insulin in [Baby L]'s blood and the reading was so high that it was actually at the limits of the reading that the machinery was capable of delivering.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There was no correspondingly high level of C-peptide. You'll remember what I told you yesterday about there should be a correlation between C-peptide and insulin. It's natural that when you are producing your own insulin, you will also be producing C-peptide, and if your insulin level is high, your Cpeptide level will be high, if your insulin level is low, your C-peptide level will be low, but the C-peptide level was within the normal range. So off the scale or at the limit of the scale for insulin, normal C-peptide.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The only explanation for that anomaly is that what was being measured was synthetic insulin, so somebody poisoned [Baby L] with insulin. He was not being prescribed it, but it is a drug that's readily available in the locked fridge in the neonatal unit and it happens to be in the same fridge as the total parenteral nutrition bags, those liquid feed bags. Do you remember, I showed you an animation of one of those bags yesterday? It was yellow coloured.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So it follows that somebody certainly gave unauthorised insulin to [Baby L]. There is an infusion therapy prescription sheet in [Baby L]'s medical records. I'm just going to show you that. It is page 17948 as you can see.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: This is a written record of the dextrose bag being fed to [Baby L]. What it shows is that the -- on this shift, the bag was running from 11 o'clock on 8 April when it had been set up by Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You can see at the top there, there are two prescriptions that have been written for 10% dextrose at 11 o'clock -- or even three, actually. In the doctor's signature column you can see the same doctor has signed, it's Dr Bhowmick(?). And you can see that the difference is the calculation. Duration of infusion: in the top line it says 4.2mls per hour, middle 3.6, and then settling on 4.4.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It was set up by Lucy Letby and Nurse Davies.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think I said -- 11 o'clock is the time of the prescription, the infusion is timed as having been started at midday and you can see it in that far right column.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We say that Lucy Letby added insulin to that bag of dextrose. She did it deliberately to kill [Baby L]. She had failed to kill [Baby F], and so she increased the dose. You'll remember, I gave you the level of insulin that was measured in [Baby F]'s blood sample, and in round terms, I don't remember off the top of my head the precise figure, but it's about half what was found in [Baby L]'s blood. That was 4,000 and something; this was 9,999.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, Lucy Letby had been present at [Baby L]'s birth and she cared for him during the first day of his life on 8 April. She would have been aware of his mild hypoglycaemia and volunteered later that day to complete an additional day shift on 9 April. We say that, in effect, she saw the opportunity to complete what she had attempted with [Baby F]. So on the day of his birth, we've just seen the prescription, dextrose.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby L]'s blood sugar remained dangerously low through the day shift on 9 April, despite further infusions of what in effect is sugar. At 4.30 that afternoon, the supplement required reached 12.5% and that necessitated a new replacement infusion bag because these bags are all specific concentrations.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Nurses Griffith and Letby were in the process of completing that task at 4.30 when [Baby L]'s twin, [Baby M], was suddenly taken ill, and Nurse Belinda Simcock took over so that they could both attend to [Baby M] and Belinda Simcock confirms that she actually connected the new bag for [Baby L].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So far as the expert evidence is concerned, the essence of the expert evidence is that this was a case of insulin poisoning and that it must have been administered intravenously to [Baby L] through his liquid feed. As I said before, the level of insulin was probably greater than the range that the machinery could measure, either that or it's a coincidence that it just happened to be the maximum that the machine could measure. And we suggest that the evidence will leave only the possibility that someone put insulin directly into the liquid feed.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: If we're right about that, the issue will be who did it. And in answering that question, then you may care to look at what happened in all the other cases.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: During her police interview, Lucy Letby agreed that she was aware of [Baby L]'s low blood sugar levels. She confirmed that she knew that prolonged low blood sugar could cause severe brain damage or even death. She confirmed that insulin on the unit was kept in a locked fridge, together with a variety of other drugs, and that the keys to the lock were passed among staff as and when needed. There was no specific keyholder, nor was a record kept of who had the keys at any given time.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She agreed that the insulin could not have been administered accidentally. She denied being responsible. Her only explanation was that it must have already been in one of the bags that [Baby L] was receiving. Well, for reasons we'll explore in evidence, ladies and gentlemen, we say that is not a credible suggestion.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby M], count 16. [Baby M], born just after [Baby L]. He was born in good condition and there were no concerns. He didn't need any assistance with his breathing and there was no evidence of infection.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He was classified as a special care baby as opposed to a high dependency baby within the neonatal unit. The reason he was in the higher level of room was because he was with his brother, which I'm sure you'll understand is something that will be arranged if at all possible.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby M] suffered an unexpected life-threatening event at about 4 pm on 9 April at the time his brother's blood sugar was dangerously low. Without warning, [Baby M]'s heart rate and breathing dropped dramatically and he required full resuscitation by the medical staff. He came close to death. Yet 4 hours later, having been resuscitated, he was breathing unsupported in air. So you'll remember, I'm sure, when I introduced the case to you just before lunch on Monday, I was telling you that one of the notable features of this case isn't just the speed of collapse but the speed of recovery, which defies the normal experience of the doctors.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: During the day shift in notes that she wrote up at the end of the shift, Mary Griffith wrote that at 11 o'clock [Baby M] had had a small posset, which those of you with kids will be familiar with, even if you're not familiar with the term, you'll be familiar with what it is. It's almost like a mouth vomit, just a little bit of sick, the sort of thing that you tend to get on the shoulder of your best dress or your best suit jacket. It doesn't happen at other times, of course, but you'll be familiar with what I'm talking about.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 12.15 it was noted by Mary Griffith that [Baby M]'s stomach was a little distended and his work of breathing was increased. At 12.30 there was an aspirate of 5 millilitres of stomach acid with partially digested milk, but he was fed, his temperature reverted to normal and he settled. And in the next feed the aspirate was 1.5 millilitres and bile-stained, which was then shown to the registrar and [Baby M] was put nil by mouth at that stage.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 2.30, fluid with bile in was aspirated from [Baby M]'s stomach. He wasn't fed again between that time and 4 pm, and you'll remember he collapsed at just after that time, but it follows from that that he cannot have choked on his stomach contents because there was nothing in his stomach. So that cannot be the cause for his collapse.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 3.30, so before his collapse, a fluid bag was attached to [Baby M], and at 3.45 he received intravenous antibiotics, and according to the notes, they were given to him by either Nurse Griffith or Lucy Letby. And so it is that Lucy Letby had the opportunity to interfere with [Baby M]'s well-being under the cover of legitimate care.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Digital records suggest that actually, when you're deciding who it was that dealt with [Baby M] at 3.45, digital records suggest that Mary Griffith was using a computer at that precise moment.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 4 o'clock, according to Mary Griffith, both she and Lucy Letby were preparing the dextrose infusion for [Baby L] with their backs to [Baby M], so the hypoglycaemic [Baby L] needed more sugar, and Nurse Griffith and Lucy Letby preparing the infusion, backs to [Baby M].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: According to what Mary Griffith said, they'd been doing for less than 10 minutes. The way this is done is one nurse acts as the person doing it and the other acts as a checker and the nurse who is carrying out the infusion, the hands-on role in the infusion, has to scrub up and make themselves sterile. Okay? And it was Nurse Mary Griffith who was the sterile nurse, so Lucy Letby had the role of checker.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Whilst Nurse Griffith was making herself sterile, [Baby M]'s monitor alarmed and Lucy Letby was first to the cot. And such was the emergency that the doctors were called urgently to help.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Nurse B] was also on duty near nursery 1 at this time. The way she remembers it is that Lucy Letby was standing with her at a computer when the alarm activated and she says that Lucy Letby was first to the cot and Lucy Letby immediately told the other nurses that [Baby M] wasn't breathing.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The way Belinda Simcock remembers it is that Lucy Letby was with Mary Griffith making up a solution at the time [Baby M] collapsed and that no one else was in the room. Well, the consultant, Dr Ravi Jayaram -- [redacted] -- he attended and he noticed unusual patches of discolouration on [Baby M]'s skin, which he thought particularly noticeable because of [Baby M]'s south Asian skin tone.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He thought the patches most unusual because normally, if a baby arrests, if they have a cardiac arrest and there's not enough oxygen moving round the body, the baby is uniformly pale, grey or blue. What he saw was what he thought was similar to what he'd seen during the resuscitations of [Babies A & B].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do you remember the first two babies?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby M] did not respond well to resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Treatment was about to be withdrawn after the injection of six doses of adrenaline -- six doses in 25 minutes -- when all of a sudden, he improved. And Dr Jayaram just couldn't find a cause for this sudden collapse, but the discolouration he'd seen caused him to suspect air embolism, an injection of air into the bloodstream.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: As a result of his collapse, the shift leader, [Nurse B], transferred [Baby M]'s care to Lucy Letby, who became his
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: designated nurse. At 9.14, Lucy Letby noticed that [Baby M] was tensing his limbs, curling his fingers and toes and rotating his hands and feet inwards.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And that sort of sign or those sorts of signs are indicative of brain damage or starvation of oxygen to the brain. And you will remember, I'm sure, similar observations in the case of [Baby J].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: On the night shift that followed, the nursing notes record that by 3.30 am [Baby M] was very active. He'd had a remarkably speedy recovery from his near death experience. He did suffer further desaturations on that shift, and in particular at 7.15 as the day shift was about to start.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Again, the independent paediatricians have looked at this case. Dr Evans would not have expected such a prompt recovery had the cause been infection or some sort of lung problem. As a cause for [Baby M]'s collapse, he favoured either airway obstruction or air embolus, and it may well be that, subject to the eyewitness evidence of Nurses Griffith, Simcock and [Nurse B], air obstruction is an unlikely possibility.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Bohin excluded a number of other potential causes of collapse and agreed with Dr Evans that the most likely cause of [Baby M]'s collapse was air embolus or airway obstruction.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: A paediatric neurologist called Dr Stavros Stivaros reviewed a brain scan obtained from [Baby M] some time later, on 27 May 2016, and found brain damage which was in his opinion most likely caused by his cardio-respiratory collapse on 9 April.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When Lucy Letby's home was searched following her arrest 2 years after this incident, the handwritten log of drugs administered during [Baby M]'s collapse was found.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just so you understand what I'm talking about, in emergency resuscitation when drugs are being given to an infant who is potentially in terminal decline, there isn't somebody there standing, making careful notes in the medical records. The way it's done, tends to be done, is on a piece of loose paper. Someone will keep a note, so they're rough notes, and the rough notes are then taken and transposed into the medical records after the emergency has ended. Okay?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So what the police found at Lucy Letby's house was that emergency -- I won't say panicked, because it wasn't panicked, but the emergency record of how many doses of adrenaline were being given to [Baby M].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In her diary, Lucy Letby also made a note, and I'll just show you that:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "LD [long day] extra..."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do you remember me telling you that she had volunteered for this shift?:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "... twin(s) resus."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: On being interviewed, Lucy Letby said that she remembered [Baby M]'s collapse. She agreed that she had connected him to a fluid bag at 3 pm. She agreed that she'd co-signed for medication at 3.45 pm, but could not be sure whether she or Mary Griffith had administered it.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said that she was alerted to [Baby M]'s collapse by an alarm sounding and commenced resuscitation immediately. She thought she must have taken the notes, which she accepted had been written by somebody else, so these are the emergency notes, if you like, the rough notes. Someone else wrote them, not she. She thought she had taken them home by accident and simply noted what had happened in her diary. So that was her explanation.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She denied that the notes were a souvenir and she denied deliberately trying to harm [Baby M]. She could think of no reason how [Baby M] could have suffered an air embolism.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We suggest, ladies and gentlemen, the prosecution suggest, that the cases of [Babies E & F] and [Babies L & M] are similar in that one each of those two pairs of twins suffered insulin poisoning and the other suffered an intravenous air embolism. And what are the chances of that happening innocently?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We suggest that coincidences like that simply do not happen innocently. Someone was responsible and we suggest the only credible candidate is Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The 14th child, please, ladies and gentlemen. This is [Baby N]. You'll find his name in the indictment at counts 17, 18 and 19. Count 17 relates to 3 June.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Counts 18 and 19 refer both to 15 June, 18 being between 7.15 and 7.30 in the morning, and 19 being at about 3 pm that afternoon.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby N] was born on 2 June. He was 34 weeks and 4 days gestation and therefore was 2 weeks and 3 days short of being classified as a full term baby. He weighed 1.67 kilos and it was known that his mother was a carrier of haemophilia, which I'm sure you know is a blood-clotting disorder. So because of that,
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: because of the knowledge of his mother's status, [Baby N] was admitted to the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Following his birth, he quickly stabilised and, that evening, his clinical condition was described as excellent. The prosecution say that there are, as you can see from the indictment, three separate occasions on which Lucy Letby tried to kill him.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby N]'s haemophilia is an important feature of his case. Many, if not most, people know that haemophilia makes someone more prone to bleeding for either no reason or a trivial reason. And it is clear from the medical notes that that's what the medical and the nursing staff at the Countess of Chester thought at the time. They were wrong.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Subsequent investigation has shown that [Baby N] has a mild version of haemophilia, and children with his mild level of haemophilia rarely bleed for no reason.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Children of his age at the time of these events do not bleed for no reason and, most importantly, blood in the throat of a child with his level of haemophilia does not occur for no reason. It doesn't happen spontaneously.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: But we allege that Lucy Letby thought that [Baby N]'s haemophilia give her cover to attack him because if she caused a bleed, it would be put down to the haemophilia.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And she was right.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Count 17. The night shift of 2 to 3 June. Christopher Booth was the designated nurse for [Baby N] on that night shift, and [Baby N] was in room number 1. The nursing staff working that night, the other nursing staff, were Melanie Taylor, Lucy Letby, Sophie Ellis and the nursery nurse Valerie Thomas.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: They all came on duty at 7.30. From 8 o'clock onwards Lucy Letby was texting her friends. She exhibited an interest in [Baby N], and in one text that she sent at 8 o'clock to her off-duty friend [Nurse E], she said:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "We've got a baby with haemophilia."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She then sent a further text saying:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Everyone bit panicked by seems (sic) of things, although baby appears fine."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Four minutes later she sent a text saying that she was going to Google haemophilia. Seven minutes later, she texted [Nurse E]:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Complex condition, yes 50:50 chance antenatally."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: No doubt this is what her Google research had told her and it appears therefore that Lucy Letby thought [Baby N] was lucky to be alive.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Jennifer Loughnane examined [Baby N] at 10.55 that night. He was presenting well and she had no concerns.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Nurse Booth, Christopher Booth, confirmed that [Baby N] was stable until he went for his break in the early hours, at about 1 o'clock. And you know the drill now, ladies and gentlemen. The practice when a nurse goes on a break is they ask a colleague to keep an eye on the baby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Nurse Booth cannot now remember who he asked. When asked about it, Nurse Taylor had no recollection of being asked but thought it might have been someone already in nursery 1. Well, Lucy Letby didn't fall into that category, she'd been allotted two babies to care for in room 4. You know from one of the other cases what she thought about being in room 4.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 1.05, so 5 minutes after Chris Booth had gone on his break, [Baby N] experienced a sudden deterioration in his oxygen saturation levels as they fell from 99% at 1 o'clock to 40%, which is a life-threatening level.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: More unusually, for such a small baby, he was described as crying and screaming. And Dr Loughnane responded to the emergency call, [Baby N] recovered quickly, and Dr Loughnane was then called away by another emergency bleep to go and deal with somebody else.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There's no entry in the medical or the nursing records recording who alerted the doctor to [Baby N]'s condition. But neither of the other nurses on duty that night -- we've excluded Christopher Booth because he'd gone on his break, the other two were Melanie Taylor -- they don't remember having been asked to take over and alerting Dr Loughnane that [Baby N] was unwell.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Evans, Dr Dewi Evans, believes that [Baby N]'s deterioration was consistent with some kind of inflicted injury, which caused pain or severe pain/distress and destabilised him. His recovery was extremely prompt, which is not what one would expect if his deterioration was due to infection or bleeding.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Evans concluded that [Baby N]'s screaming was consistent with inflicted injury or him having received an injection of air.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Bohin agreed. She said such a profound desaturation followed by a rapid recovery, in the absence of any painful or uncomfortable procedure, suggested an inflicted, painful stimulus. She also said:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "This is life-threatening. He was also noted to be screaming and apparently cried for 30 minutes. This is most unusual. I have never observed a premature neonate to scream."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby didn't leave it there. I'll come to the other two incidents on 15 June.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Twelve days later, there were two separate incidents on that day shift. To put what happened into context, we suggest that it's important to note that Lucy Letby had been [Baby N]'s designated nurse on the previous day shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just going back to the 14th for a moment, on that day shift, the 14th, [Baby N] had been doing really well.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He was demanding expressed breast milk and taking more than the required volumes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He was almost ready to go home and the only thing that was holding him back was jaundice. Overnight he was in nursery 3. At the beginning of the night shift, so this is the night shift of 14th to the 15th, just after Lucy Letby had handed him over to Jennifer Jones-Key, [Baby N] was described as being "very unsettled".
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 1 in the morning he was found to be pale, mottled and veiny, with slight abdominal distension, so swelling. The mottling persisted, he was monitored by staff through the early hours and he desaturated to the low 80s on a number of occasions but selfcorrected without any intervention from the nursing staff.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He was seen on three separate occasions by the registrar, [Dr A], who saw nothing of concern: no signs of injury or blood but, as a precaution, the decision was taken to test for infection.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was to be [Baby N]'s designated nurse again on 15 June. The use of her phone suggests that she was awake by 5.10 that morning. Later, [Nurse E] texted her to tell her that things on the unit were busy and "[Baby N] screened, looks like shit".
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was in for her day shift by 7.12. We know that because she texted the registrar, [Dr A], to tell him that she had "escaped 1", in other words escaped room 1 and was "back in 3", room 3.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The electronic records of the hospital on the door fob suggest that she passed through the fob-controlled security door, the first one at 7.10 and the second one at 7.12. And the other nurses working on the day shift were [Nurse B], Bernadette Butterworth, Minna Lappalainen, and the nursery nurses Vicky Blamire and Janet Pearce. [Nurse E] stayed in beyond the end of her night shift for a couple of hours.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Now, Jennifer Jones-Key, who had been the nurse to whom Lucy Letby had handed over [Baby N] the night before, was coming off as Lucy Letby came on that morning. She described some improvement in [Baby N] up until about 7.15 when Lucy Letby arrived early for her day shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby, she says, came into the room to say hello, but when she did that, Nurse Jones-Key had her back to Lucy Letby and her back to [Baby N]. And Lucy Letby said to Jennifer Jones-Key that [Baby N] had desaturated before immediately assisting with his breathing. There was no evidence of an alarm sounding or of Lucy Letby waiting to see whether he self-corrected. [Redacted].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Dr A] was called to attend and [Baby N] was handed over to Lucy Letby as his designated nurse and transferred into nursery 1. The medical notes that were made at 8 o'clock recorded desaturations of 48%, a dangerously low level.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: During this event, an attempt was made by the registrar, [Dr A], to put an ET tube down [Baby N]'s throat. You know what I'm going to say. In his statement [Dr A] describes that he was "surprised by his anatomy more than anything else. I couldn't visualise parts of the back of his throat because of swelling."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby C]. When [Dr A] looked, he saw that there was fresh blood in [Baby N]'s throat. [Baby C], [Baby E], [Baby G] and now [Baby N]. All with the same issue.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Dr A] couldn't get the breathing tube down [Baby N]'s throat because he couldn't see the inlet to the trachea in the throat. He tried to intubate [Baby N] on three occasions.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: If we look at page 19315, please. What we've got here, ladies and gentlemen, is an intensive care chart, you can see, from the Countess of Chester. We can see highlighted a number of things. 15 June, top left.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: This chart basically divides into two. Input and output.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So the left hand -- you can see highlighted in yellow the words input and output. So what are we putting into a baby, what's the record of what we're putting in and what's coming out of the baby?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: What we see is that this record started at 9 o'clock in the morning on the 15th, so after [Baby N] had collapsed. It's about 100 minutes or so after the collapse, which coincided with Lucy Letby's arrival.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: What you have there is Lucy Letby's handwriting -- or mostly Lucy Letby's handwriting, I should say. If you look at the very right-hand column, you've got LL times 5 for those entries and then for the entry at 15.00 hours you've got [initials of Nurse B], which is [Nurse B].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So at 10 o'clock, you see it's highlighted on the left-hand column, 10, and you read across, you can see in handwriting "1ml fresh blood". That's recorded in the "NG ASP/VOMIT" column. You can't see what the column is headed in the expanded part of the chart, but those of you with better eyesight than me can probably see it -- it's completely obscured again. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it's there. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just let's put this into context. This is a baby that Lucy Letby thinks has beaten the odds, or at least beaten the evens, 50:50, making it through to a live birth, and has -- and we know she thought, and she was right, he had haemophilia but not to the extent she thought, as I will tell you in a moment.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The column that I have just highlighted before, the 1ml fresh blood, is intended to record the aspirates that are withdrawn from the stomach through the NG tube before a baby is fed. But the bleeding, other than that writing, which is Lucy Letby's handwriting, that bleeding isn't recorded anywhere in the medical notes, so in the doctor's notes. No doctor ever made a similar note. This was more than 2 hours after [Dr A] had tried to intubate [Baby N] following his collapse at 7.30.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Now, at 11.29, so an hour and a half after that note, if that note is correct and is timed correctly, at 11.29 Lucy Letby sent a Facebook message to [Dr A] telling him:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Small amounts of blood from mouth and 1ml from NG."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Which would tie in with that handwritten entry:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Looks like pulmonary bleed on X-ray."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: What that means is a bleed in the lungs, which is the sort of thing that you might get if you were a premature baby with haemophilia.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Given factor 8, wait and see."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that's the message she sent the doctor. But other than that phone message, there's no evidence that she brought the bleeding to the attention of any of the medical staff who were on the ward, which is surprising given the problems that [Baby N] had suffered with an extreme collapse at the beginning of the shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In an update recorded on the computer notes at about 1.55 that afternoon, she wrote that [Baby N] was "stiff" on handling, extending his upper limbs and arching his back. And I probably need to say no more than [Baby D] and [Baby J] to you in that respect.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You will remember similar observations with them.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: If we just have the -- sorry, having told you to get rid of it — thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 3 o'clock, 15.00 hours, if you read across, towards the right of the screen, what we have there, ladies and gentlemen, is "occluding" written, and then towards the right "3ml blood". That is, we say, Lucy Letby's handwriting. It's not [Nurse B]'s handwriting, although she has initialled it, and that coincides with a second collapse that day. This is the second of the two counts of the day.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just before 3 o'clock that afternoon, the medical staff were crash bleeped because [Baby N]'s oxygen levels had fallen this time to 44%, so again life-threatening.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Huw Mayberry was the first to respond. He was junior and was aware of the problem that the more senior doctor, [Dr A], had had that morning, trying to intubate [Baby N], and because of that, he crash bleeped the consultant, Dr Saladi. He did that at 1.59.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: While waiting for Dr Saladi to arrive, he looked into [Baby N]'s mouth, into his airway, and saw what he describes as a large swelling at the end of his epiglottis. The epiglottis is that funny thing that hangs down from the top of the back of your throat. And he could only just see the bottom of [Baby N]'s vocal cords. He had never seen anything like this in a newborn baby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: On the other hand, Dr Saladi made notes at 4.30. He recorded this:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Desaturated this afternoon at 2.50 pm with blood in the oropharynx [so that's the top of the throat] and blood in the NG tube. Improved with bagging, elective intubation planned
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: following??? Unsuccessful attempts with two registrars and two consultants. Cords difficult to visualise."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So putting that into more straightforward language, various people have tried to intubate this child but because of what looked like problems in the throat, had not been able to.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The notes made by Lucy Letby towards the end of the shift at about 6.30 record this:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "At approximately 2.50 infant became apnoeic with desaturation to 44%. Heart rate 90 beats a minute. Fresh blood noted from mouth and 3mls of blood aspirated from NG tube. Doctors crash called."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Ladies and gentlemen, [Baby N] was so unwell that attempts were made to re-intubate him, to put a tube down his throat, but [Dr A] couldn't see down the throat because the view was obscured by fresh blood.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Something, somebody, we say, had caused [Baby N] to bleed again. And it took a more specialist team who were called in to carry out the intubation.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby N] continued to be unwell throughout that day and the difficulties with ventilating him persisted, despite the experience of the doctors involved, and eventually he had to be transferred to Alder Hey Hospital in Liverpool, where he recovered quickly, following the pattern of [Baby H] and [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Again, ladies and gentlemen, the independent specialists, the non-Countess of Chester specialists, have looked at [Baby N]'s case. It is Dr Evans' considered opinion that the blood seen in [Baby N]'s throat had originated in [Baby N]'s throat and hadn't come up from the stomach. In Dr Evans' opinion the bleeding was not caused by the attempts to put a tube down his throat, but instead it was something before that that had caused the collapse in the first place. He placed particular significance on the presence of blood in [Baby N]'s throat before [Dr A] had first tried to insert a tube into [Baby N] at 8 that morning.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He suggested that the bleed might have been caused by thrusting an NG tube into the back of [Baby N]'s throat because [Baby N] was otherwise a stable baby who didn't suffer any spontaneous bleeds at any time as a result of his condition.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Bohin suggested only two possibilities: either inflicted trauma or a spontaneous bleed. She considered the idea of a spontaneous bleed, in other words bleeding for no reason, to be less likely because of the level of [Baby N]'s haemophilia. That
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: is a question that has since been confronted by Professor Kinsey, whose highly specialised area is blood disorders.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Bohin's view was that the likely cause of bleeding was trauma to the mouth, to the throat or to the oropharynx, this area, which was most likely from an NG tube or a suction catheter, and she thought that the injury to the epiglottis seen by the junior doctor in the afternoon supported the suggestion that there had been a further attempt to injure [Baby N].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: As I have already said, Professor Kinsey considered the significance of [Baby N]'s diagnosis of moderate haemophilia in the context of the evidence relating to his collapses and reported bleeding. She describes the first collapse at the beginning of June as dramatic with no recognised medical cause. She excluded the possibility of pulmonary haemorrhage, in other words bleeding from the lungs then coming up, causing the collapse on 15 June because, in her opinion, such bleeding would not have occurred spontaneously in a child with [Baby N]'s degree of haemophilia. So it follows, we say, that the bleeding must have been caused by trauma because the blood was seen before anybody tried to put a tube down [Baby N]'s throat.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: As a matter of interest, Dr Kinsey also rules out heavy-handed intubation as a potentially accidental cause.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When she was interviewed by the police, Lucy Letby said that she had difficulty remembering [Baby N] and she didn't think that he had been named at the time and she was right about that. She did recall an occasion when doctors had difficulty intubating [Baby N]. She agreed that she'd seen blood, but she denied being responsible for causing him harm.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She couldn't explain the injury in her notes, the one I showed you earlier from 10 o'clock in the morning on 15 June, in which she recorded aspirating more fresh blood which she had not apparently brought to the attention of anybody else at that time, at 10 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that is the case or the cases of [Baby N], and we come now to the [Babies O & P], who are often in this case referred to by witnesses by the surname [redacted].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Mr Johnson, I'm just going to enquire of the jury if you would like a break. The alternative to having a 10minute break now and then doing half an hour is just to do half an hour or thereabouts now. Are you happy...? Carry on? Good, thank you. We'll do that then. If you could finish no later than 10 to, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, of course.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So we're dealing now with counts 20 and 21. So pages 7 and 8 of the indictment -- and you'll be glad to see the indictment ends at page 8, so that's a good sign.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We allege that Lucy Letby murdered two of the three brothers who were born on Tuesday, 21 June to [Parents of Babies O, P & R]. I'll deal first with the case of [Baby O], whose murder is alleged in count 20.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby O] was born at 2.24 in the afternoon on Tuesday, 21 June at a gestational age of 33 weeks and 2 days. He weighed 2.02 kilos, which for a premature triplet is pretty good. He was in good condition and he made good progress. He remained stable up until the afternoon of Tuesday, 23 June, when he suffered what Dr Evans described as "a remarkable deterioration" and died.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: His death was 8 days after Lucy Letby had tried to kill [Baby N]. Between trying to kill [Baby N] and her attack on the [Babies O & P], Lucy Letby had been on holiday to Ibiza, so she'd not been at work.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Overnight, on 22 to 23 June -- so he was born on the 21st. So overnight on the 22nd to 23rd, [Baby O]'s designated nurse had been Sophie Ellis and the feeding chart records that when his stomach was aspirated by the NGT, there had been some partially digested milk. And Sophie Ellis had asked Dr Mayberry to check [Baby O] because his abdomen appeared slightly distended, slightly swollen. Dr Mayberry did so and had no cause for concern. That examination wasn't documented in the medical notes but it does appear in Sophie Ellis' nursing notes that were timed at 7.30, so the time of the handover.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When [Baby O]'s body was examined after his death, an injury to his liver was found, so the police went back to Dr Mayberry who had checked [Baby O]'s abdomen. They showed him the pathologist's report and asked whether he, Dr Mayberry, when he'd examined [Baby O] that morning he'd detected any symptoms to indicate either any liver issues or any damage and Dr Mayberry said no.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, Lucy Letby was working the day shift on Thursday, 23 June, and you know the form now. She came on duty at 7.30 that morning. She was the designated nurse for [Babies O & P], who were both in room 2, with another child who I will refer to as JD, for whom she was also the designated nurse. So it follows that there were three children in room 2: one was [Baby O], one was [Baby P], and the third was JD. Lucy Letby was the only nurse working in the room.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We say that gave her an open opportunity to sabotage the babies, though she did at the same time have the responsibility of supervising a student nurse called Rebecca Morgan.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Ironically, the third of the triplets, [Baby R], was in room 1, and so it appears that the doctors thought that he was the more needy of the triplets.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Other nursing staff on duty that day were Melanie Taylor, who was the shift leader, Samantha O'Brien, Christopher Booth and Yvonne Griffiths and the nursery nurse was Janet Cox.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby O] was examined again at about 9.30 by Dr Katarzyna Cooke --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm sorry about this, someone's obviously drilling something, I think. And now hammering.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
We'll carry on anyway. If you can't hear anything, just say, raise a hand.
Thank you.

Dr Cooke, Katarzyna Cooke, at 9.30 that morning, examined [Baby O]. She recorded no nursing concern, observations normal. So when you're considering whether [Baby O] had a liver injury at this stage, another doctor examined him and found no cause for concern.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby O] was getting some breathing support through Optiflow, which is the least invasive breathing support, but he was in air, so no supplemental oxygen required, just normal air under a bit of pressure. He was breathing normally, his abdomen was noted as appearing "full", but not distended, soft, non-tender. So a good sign.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby O] was being fed donated breast milk via a nasogastric tube, and there are three records of feeds made by Lucy Letby to [Baby O]: one at 8.30, one at 10.30 and one at 12.30. blocks.text: [Dr A] made a note at 1.15 in the afternoon and his note said "1 times vomit post-feed" and also "Abdomen distended" and that's why [Baby O] was put on an intravenous feed, so liquid feed, into his bloodstream rather than what they call an enteral feed, which is a traditional feed through the mouth.

blocks.text: That followed a feed given by Lucy Letby, that problem, and [Baby O]'s heart rate was up at between 160 and 170 beats a minute and his blood gases showed a low pH value, so acidic, and raised CO2, so raised carbon dioxide, which I told you [Dr A] described as not normal for a child who was breathing on his own. blocks.text: According to what [Dr A] did note, it was thought that [Baby O]'s abdominal distension, the swelling of his belly, putting it bluntly, was because of the Optiflow, because of the breathing support he was getting, so swallowing air in effect, or that it might have been the strain of passing a stool which he had been recorded as having done earlier.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: An X-ray was taken at the time. That showed a moderate amount of gas in the loops of his bowel. Do you remember that graphic of the baby yesterday that you saw with the NG tube going down into the stomach and below the diaphragm and then the stomach and the loops of bowel going down? In her note made at the end of the shift, Lucy Letby wrote this:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Reviewed by [Dr A] at 1.15. [Baby O] had vomited undigested milk. Tachycardic [which means high heart rate] and abdomen distended. NG tube placed on free drainage."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Now, putting the NG tube on free drainage, you'll remember, enables any excess gas to come out, to vent in effect:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "10 ml/kilo saline bolus."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: This is a dose of saline given as prescribed along with antibiotics. Of course saline also can -- yes:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "... given along with the antibiotics. Placed nil by mouth and abdominal X-ray performed. Observations returned to normal."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Prior to [Baby O]'s collapse, Melanie Taylor was in room 2 with [Baby O] and with Lucy Letby. While Melanie Taylor was in the room with Lucy Letby, she said to Lucy Letby of [Baby O], so figuratively if not literally pointing to [Baby O], Melanie Taylor said to Lucy Letby:

blocks.text: "He doesn't look as well now as he did earlier. Do you think we should move him back to room 1 to be safe?"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You've heard this before, haven't you? Lucy Letby did not agree. And that has echoes, doesn't it, of the final fatal collapse of [Baby I] and what Lucy Letby said to Ashleigh Hudson? So events repeating themselves.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby recorded that she had taken [Baby O]'s observations at 2.30 that afternoon. His heart and breathing rates were normal and his saturations in air, so no additional oxygen, were 100%, as good as you can get. So that's what she recorded in his notes at 2.30, but we know from her phone that at that precise moment she was sending messages over Facebook Messenger. So at the time that she was recorded as writing in the notes, actually on Facebook Messenger. The door fob entry data shows that she came into the neonatal unit at 14.39, so 9 minutes after that entry.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So whether the timing of that observation of [Baby O] is correct or accurate may be a matter that we will consider in the evidence, but whether or not there's a point there, within a few minutes of Lucy Letby coming back into the neonatal unit, as
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: evidenced by the door entry system, [Baby O] suffered his first collapse.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Melanie Taylor responded to a call for help from Lucy Letby, who was alone with [Baby O] in room number 2.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The door data suggests that the call for help must have come some time after 14.46 because that was the time that Mel Taylor came back into the unit. Anyway.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby O]'s heart rate and saturations had dropped to dangerously low levels and a breathing tube was inserted by the doctors and he was successfully resuscitated and then kept on a ventilator.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Some time later, at about 3.50, [Baby O] desaturated again and [Dr B] and [Dr A] removed the ET tube and replaced it as a precaution. Lucy Letby's notes written later that day suggest that it was she who called for help, so yet again she's the one.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby O] suffered yet a further collapse at 4.15, which again required resuscitation, including cardiac compressions, and tragically those efforts were unsuccessful and were withdrawn at 17.47 and [Baby O] died soon after.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: During this episode, Dr Brearey, the consultant, noted that [Baby O] had an area of discoloured skin on the right side of his chest wall, which was -- the medical term he used is purpuric. That means a rash which looks like small spots of blood on the skin.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Brearey, the consultant, noticed a persistent rash at 4.30, which had disappeared by 5.15, and consequently he concluded that it wasn't purpura, as he understands that to be, and was unsure what had caused it. He was particularly concerned, was Dr Brearey, about [Baby O]'s death because [Baby O] had been clinically stable before these events. His collapse was so sudden and he didn't respond as he should have done to resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: After the shift, Lucy Letby sent a variation of text messages to [Dr A], the registrar, on Facebook at just before 9 pm. She also communicated with her friend, [Nurse E]. She told [Nurse E] that [Baby O] had died and said the following. She suggested that he had:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Had a big tummy overnight, but just ballooned after lunch and went from there."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: A post-mortem examination took place and Dr Kokai, the pathologist, found free, unclotted -- in other words liquid -blood in the peritoneal space which had come from the liver. The
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: peritoneal space is the cavity in your abdomen. There was damage in multiple locations, both on and in [Baby O]'s liver, and the blood that was found in the peritoneal cavity had come from the liver.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Kokai certified death on the basis of natural causes and intra-abdominal bleeding. He observed that the cause of the bleeding could have been asphyxia, trauma or vigorous resuscitation. Of course, it wouldn't occur to him that perhaps a nurse had assaulted a child on a neonatal unit. That, however, did occur to other experts.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Evans reviewed the case and he concluded that [Baby O]'s death was the result of a combination of intravenous air embolus, in other words air into the bloodstream, and trauma. Dr Evans' view was that the liver injury was not consistent with vigorous CPR. His view was that the liver damage would have occurred before the collapse and contributed to it and was probably the reason for his symptoms through the morning. As for the air in the bowel loops, Dr Evans concluded that that was consistent with air going down the NGT.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Bohin noted intravascular gas, in other words gas in the bloodstream, in the post-mortem X-rays and concluded that, together with the chest wall discolouration seen by Dr Brearey, that was indicative of air having been injected into [Baby O]'s circulation.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She also thought that the swelling of the abdomen of [Baby O] was due to excess gas given down the nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The reviewing pathologist, Dr Andreas Marnerides, thought that the liver injuries were most likely the result of some impact trauma, so in brutal terms an assault, not CPR. He thought that the excess air -- he thought that excess air via the nasogastric tube likely led to stimulation of the vagal (sic) nerve, which has an effect on the heart rate and would also have compromised [Baby O]'s bleeding.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: He couldn't say whether it was either of those factors in isolation or in combination which had caused [Baby O]'s death and he certified the cause of death to be:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Inflicted traumatic injury to the liver and profound gastric and intestinal distension following acute excessive injection or infusion of air via a nasogastric tube and air embolus."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So we've got a combination of three here, ladies and gentlemen: air into the bloodstream, air down the tube, and some sort of impact injury to [Baby O]'s liver causing bleeding.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In her police interviews, Lucy Letby said that she responded to [Baby O]'s alarm at 1.15 and she found that he had vomited. She said the alarm sounded again at 2.40. blocks.text: She said that his abdomen just kept swelling and suggested that sometimes babies can gulp air when they are receiving assistance from Optiflow, as [Baby O] was.
